cells.tense: You are moving on purpose, and the method you follow is showing up in results.
cells.ask: Name the goal you're moving toward and do one action today that proves you've started. Put it where you can see it before the day ends.
cells.core:
You are moving on purpose now. No one has to tell you to practice — the method is already in your hands, and you can see the difference it makes. The work shows. You keep the aim clear and keep taking the next step, which is why the results keep arriving.

What this balance is free to feed next: break the next structure that needs breaking. You can already picture one goal that has been sitting there. Name it and take one step today that would not have happened if you were still waiting. That kind of action is simple and slow, and it is how you find out which structures really needed to go.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving toward the goal without being pushed.
cells.verb: doing the work in a way that can be watched
cells.place: the line between starting and finishing, where the next move is chosen

cells.tense: You'll push the method harder because a finish line still hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Take one goal off tomorrow's list and put it on today's. If it has no write-up, block the time anyway and stop there.
cells.core:
You are pressing the method harder because a finish line still has not arrived. Each talk you have becomes a chance to check the plan, each open hour a chance to prove the work is working. You are living in the version where it finally lands, so you keep pressing. The pressing costs you the thing it was for.

There is a different action today: choose one goal and put it on today instead of tomorrow. Then stop and let the hours take it. That is not giving up. When a project is done, setting it down is the next structural move — you let it hold on its own instead of standing over it. Try that with one thing, today, and see what an empty block of time is like.
cells.sheetLine: You're planning the next win instead of living in today's.
cells.verb: doing the work in a way that can be watched

cells.tense: You stopped walking because a goal from before was already there and you never moved from it.
cells.ask: Pick one goal you still care about and do one small action toward it today, even badly.
cells.core:
You stopped walking. Somewhere back a goal landed and the momentum did not carry forward — you can still feel the old aim, but your attention is elsewhere, and the daily method that used to move you is not in your hands. The skill has not gone anywhere. The movement stopped.

What can bring it back is fairness, not force. Put one goal that still matters in front of you and do a small action toward it — badly is fine — today. That is not a push. It is a fair exchange: you give the goal one action, it gives you a signal, and you can see whether the direction is still yours. Nobody is asking for the whole thing. Just the next move.
cells.sheetLine: The old goal is still there and the movement stopped.
cells.verb: doing the work in a way that can be watched

cells.tense: You are already pressing this forward, but you tell it like it is proceeding on its own.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to yourself or someone, that you are the one picking the next move.
cells.core:
You are already pressing this forward. The practicing is happening — you show up, you do the method, you decide with precision — and you tell it as though the thing were running on its own. It is moving. The work is taking shape. Things are progressing. The one picking the next move is not in the story you tell.

A smaller, earlier move brings it back. You can imagine; that part is not in question here. Say once, plainly, "I decided this" about one part of the project you have been calling the process. Your dreaming and your drive are the same line seen from two angles, and stepping back into imagining shows you were behind it the whole time. That step is available today, with no one else there.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering this. You just call it the process.

attempts.check: I have taken 'rigorous inquiry, method, embodied clarity' and rendered it in Drive as scheduling practice sessions for a future already planned in the head; the method might function together with routines and other people more than the record states. A reader could say the planning is how they show up reliably, not a way of keeping momentum at a distance, and I would accept that without changing the ask. The ask — take one goal off tomorrow's list and put it on today's — still teaches whether the person can act without the written future, so it survives a wrong read. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you've already run the whole thing in your head'; it sounds clean but could overclaim an interior event I cannot see, so I am not writing it.
